edges.effect_quant: The strongest modern randomized evidence supports oral spironolactone as an effective treatment for persistent acne in women, with older trial and review literature pointing in the same direction.
edges.population: adolescent and adult females with acne vulgaris
edges.mechanism: Spironolactone reduces androgen-driven sebum production and can blunt one of the core hormonal pathways that sustains acne in many women. That makes it especially relevant for persistent facial acne with an endocrine pattern rather than as a universal first-line therapy for every acne presentation.
edges.summary: The SAFA randomized trial showed a real clinical benefit for oral spironolactone in women with persistent acne, reinforcing the older controlled evidence that made the drug a longstanding off-label dermatology option. The literature update also concludes that the overall efficacy signal is credible, so this edge belongs in the practical treatment category rather than the speculative one.
edges.caveats: Most direct evidence is in women, and tolerability, pregnancy considerations, and potassium-monitoring context matter in real-world use. This is a meaningful therapeutic edge, but it is not the right fit for every acne phenotype or every patient.

evidence.notes: Effectiveness of spironolactone for women with acne vulgaris (SAFA) in England and Wales: pragmatic, multicentre, phase 3, double blind, randomised controlled trial.

evidence.citation: Muhlemann MF et al 1986 Br J Dermatol
evidence.notes: Oral spironolactone: an effective treatment for acne vulgaris in women.
